title: Starch Hydrolysis Test
principle: Organisms that produce the extracellular enzyme amylase can hydrolyze starch incorporated into an agar medium into smaller sugars. Flooding the plate with iodine reveals this: iodine forms a blue-black complex with intact starch but leaves a clear zone where starch has already been broken down around growth.
purpose: Differentiates starch-hydrolyzing (amylase-positive) organisms from those that cannot break down starch, used as one identifying character among various bacterial and some fungal groups.

procedure.instruction: Inoculate a starch agar plate with the test organism as a single streak or spot.
Incubate at the appropriate temperature until visible growth appears.
Flood the plate with iodine solution.
Observe the area immediately surrounding the growth for a clear zone against the blue-black background of intact starch.

positiveResult: A clear (colorless) zone surrounding the growth against the blue-black iodine-starch background, indicating starch was hydrolyzed.
negativeResult: No clear zone — the blue-black color extends up to the edge of growth, indicating starch was not hydrolyzed.
interpretation: A positive result indicates amylase production capable of breaking down starch in the surrounding medium; the zone size can loosely reflect the extent of enzyme diffusion and activity, though it is not typically used as a precise quantitative measure.
precautions: Add iodine only after adequate growth has developed; flooding too early can make a weak positive hard to distinguish.
Read the plate promptly after adding iodine, since the color reaction fades over time.
limitations: Iodine staining is qualitative; it does not directly quantify amylase activity level.
Heavy confluent growth can make the clear zone difficult to see if the streak is too dense or too close to adjacent growth.
